summary: Researchers at the University of Tübingen asked 84 people to rate 123 wild bird species, identifying the Eurasian blackbird as most pleasant with an average rating of 4.52 out of 5.

While people intuitively expected simple, repetitive sounds to be most pleasant, the study showed that more intricate birdsongs actually received higher ratings, alongside preferences for softer vocalizations with narrower frequency ranges.

Among other species, the European goldfinch scored 4.26, followed by the European robin at 4.04 and the blue tit at 3.92, whereas the barn owl's raspy screech received the lowest average rating at 1.32.

Dr. Olga Feher of the University of Warwick warned that focusing only on charismatic, melodious birds could negatively impact conservation efforts for less pleasant-sounding species, while Dr. Robert Lachlan of Royal Holloway noted biological factors likely influence these preferences.

Future research aims to determine if these human preferences hold consistent across different cultures and environments, as Randler suggested the findings could help city planners design better acoustic environments by integrating natural sounds like birdsong into urban spaces.
title: Study Finds Certain Birdsong Qualities Are More Pleasing to Humans

Biologist Hilton used scissors to cut the roughly 6-foot-long fishing line while a colleague stabilized the bird. Wire cutters removed the hook during a procedure taking about five minutes.

summary: On Friday, President Donald Trump attacked Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar after she released a campaign ad criticizing his immigration policy, claiming she 'got a little bit soft on the border' and questioning her political success without his support.

In the ad, Salazar warned that the administration's deportation efforts had "gone too far," citing that 50 percent of Customs Enforcement detainees in July lacked criminal convictions. She characterized the message as a "warning" to the President rather than an attack.

Representing a 74-percent Hispanic district that Trump won, Salazar is seeking re-election against Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. She urged the President to model his immigration approach on Lincoln or Reagan to provide a "dignified life" for those in the country.

Criticism from Democrats and in Congress followed the ad, with journalist Gary Legum suggesting her polling numbers must be "terrrrrrible" to justify rebuking Trump by name. Salazar maintains she intended to caution the President regarding his administration's current immigration enforcement strategies.

As the midterms approach, the effectiveness of Salazar's strategy to distance herself from Trump remains uncertain. She faces a complex balancing act, attempting to satisfy her constituents while challenging the leader of her own party on a central campaign issue.
title: Maria Elvira Salazar Warns Trump His Immigration Policies Could Cost Hispanic Support

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Paramount ’s merger push as stalled, stressing that four state attorneys general are “not on board” and have “blocked” a quick settlement, with “hit a wall” conveying frustration and institutional resistance.
Right-Leaning coverage instead emphasizes a $1.5 billion California production investment as a costly “concession” that could clear a regulatory “hurdle,” subtly highlighting government pressure.
Center coverage presents detailed bargaining, including a 30-film pledge and possible penalty, without escalating the conflict.
The dividing line is whether officials represent necessary antitrust scrutiny or obstruction; all perspectives agree the merger faces legal obstacles and depends on negotiated commitments.
summary: On Sunday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Paramount and California Attorney General Rob Bonta are in advanced settlement negotiations over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger, including a $1.5 billion investment in California production.
Bonta leads a 12-state coalition that sued to block the merger two months ago, stating Thursday he sought to 'step into that breach' after the United States DOJ performed an inadequate review.

Paramount would face a $30 million penalty for each film falling short of production goals, while proposals also include independent content monitoring of CBS News and CNN, plus potential divestiture of Miramax.
New York Attorney General Letitia James and Connecticut Attorney General William Tong remain holdouts, seeking 'structural remedies' such as cable channel divestitures from the settlement.
The Block the Merger Coalition announced protests across Los Angeles and New York this week, calling the potential deal 'an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction.
title: Paramount, California AG discuss concessions including $1.5 billion investment, WSJ reports

Center coverage is more explanatory, stressing “unfounded claims,” warning signs, and the mistrial.
All emphasize the children’s deaths, Patrick’s grief, forgiveness, and public scrutiny, reflecting wider tensions between mental-health context and punishment.
summary: On Sunday, September 20, 2026, Patrick Clancy gave his first televised interview to CBS News' "60 Minutes," addressing the grief of losing his three children and his public criticism of online conspiracy theories.

The interview followed a mistrial declared September 4, 2026, after jurors deadlocked in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who was accused of strangling their three children in 2023 while experiencing postpartum psychosis.

Patrick, who revealed he once struggled with suicidal thoughts, expressed forgiveness for Lindsay, stating "I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive, so I'm sure there were things I didn't see."
Dr. Rachel Danis, whom Patrick married in April 2026, joined the interview to defend their relationship while attempting to support him and honor the memory of his children.

Addressing online rumors, Patrick called claims that he was connected to the deaths "deeply harmful," arguing they distract from perinatal health conversations and have caused real harm to those involved.
title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her for killing children in first televised interview

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the advertisement as a serious racial-harm failure, foregrounding “ KKK ,” “lynching,” and terms like “racist ad” while linking the imagery to Black history and corporate responsibility.

Right-Leaning coverage treats the same resemblance as an “optical illusion” or “harmless ad,” portraying critics as a “woke mob,” “race baiters,” or “hysterics,” and Converse’s removal as “caving” to ideological pressure.
The pivotal divide is whether visual impact outweighs intent—and whether the apology represents accountability or capitulation.

Center coverage more cautiously emphasizes an unintended association and “controversy.” All agree the ad was withdrawn and Converse apologized, reflecting wider disputes over racial symbolism and cancel culture.
summary: On Friday, Converse removed a social media advertisement featuring K-pop star Karina of Aespa after critics argued the lighting and composition resembled Ku Klux Klan hoods and lynching imagery. The Nike-owned brand issued a formal apology, stating it understood why the image was 'deeply upsetting.'

The Chuck 70 X campaign, launched globally August 27, featured Karina standing under a star-shaped spotlight wearing a white skirt. Social media users claimed the lighting created a triangular silhouette resembling a KKK hood, while dangling shoes evoked lynching imagery, intensifying when a separate Converse x Palmes collaboration surfaced showing sneakers hanging from a tree.

Chicago-Based photographer Stephanie Schwartz wrote that 'whoever did this ad knew EXACTLY what they were doing,' while civil rights attorney Lee Merritt, based in Texas, stated the apology 'doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step.' Both critiqued the company's vetting process.

Converse Chief Executive Officer Aaron Cain acknowledged in a memo that 'The images should not have been used' and committed to reviewing internal processes. The company confirmed removal from all social channels and pledged to eliminate the advertisement everywhere it appeared.

Target pulled a Halloween costume last month after critics said it evoked racist minstrel caricatures, while Urban Outfitters sold a Kent State sweatshirt in 2014 with blood stains referencing a deadly shooting. These recurring brand failures reflect mounting pressure on retailers to improve cultural sensitivity in advertising oversight.
title: Converse Apologizes and Pulls Sneaker ad that Critics Said Included Racist Imagery

bias: Coverage converges on more than 25,000 transfers involving roughly 35 countries, but diverges in framing: left-leaning accounts use “secretly,” “expelled,” and “mass expulsions” to stress opacity, public payments, weak destination ties, and potentially abusive treatment; right-leaning accounts use “deported,” “secret agreements,” and “legal limbo,” emphasizing enforcement, the administration’s claim that some migrants could not legally be returned home, and that most went to Mexico.
Center coverage foregrounds investigative methods and scale.

The sharpest divide concerns whether third-country transfers represent problematic coercion or a claimed legal-administrative response, while all perspectives highlight secrecy and the policy’s international reach.
summary: On Monday, an investigation revealed the United States has deported more than 25,000 people to 35 countries under secretive agreements with nations having no ties to the migrants, according to Forbidden Stories.

The State Department's Office of Remigration, created in May 2025, manages these deals using visa bans to pressure countries into accepting deportees while earmarking $410 million to facilitate returns.

Internal State Department records show $81 million was earmarked for signatory governments, while more than $178 million went to the International Organisation for Migration and $123 million to UNHCR.

Lawyers told AFP that deportees are held without charge in countries where they have no ties or rights, describing the situation as a "legal black hole." Eswatini has received 32 people since July 2025.

Beyond the majority sent to Mexico, the administration has finalized agreements in 27 countries across Africa, Latin America, and the Pacific, with Forbidden Stories reporting the administration approached 49 of Africa's 54 nations.
title: US has deported 25,000 people to third countries under secretive deals, report shows

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the proposed six-to-seven-month financial restrictions as an “attack” that could “paralyze” or “dismantle” the ICC, stressing damage to international accountability.

Right-Leaning coverage instead portrays them as “defending Israel” and resisting a “corrupt and politicized” court, with Netanyahu’s arrest warrant as the pivotal trigger; terms like “high-intensity” and “crippling” cast the policy as decisive.
Center coverage de-emphasizes partisan judgment, foregrounding “sources say” and uncertainty while calling the move an escalation.

All perspectives emphasize broad sanctions against the institution, potential operational disruption, and tensions over Israeli leaders and the Afghanistan investigation—reflecting wider divides over sovereignty, accountability, and Israel.
summary: The Trump administration is preparing to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court , the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, with measures forbidding most transactions after a grace period of six to seven months.
Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant received ICC arrest warrants in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, prompting this wider sanctions campaign by the Trump administration.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July the administration would dismantle the court "brick by brick" if necessary. Washington has already sanctioned former chief prosecutor Karim Khan and ICC president Tomoko Akane.

Officials said measures could be finalized this week during the United Nations General Assembly. The European Union has considered activating its Blocking Statute to shield European businesses from United States sanctions.

Rubio argued that the ICC's pursuit of non-member officials creates a dangerous precedent for the United States. Neither the United States nor Israel belongs to the ICC, though Japan and European governments have pledged protection.
title: Trump Administration Prepares to Sanction the International Criminal Court, WSJ Reports

summary: By September 11, Mossgiel Organic Dairy sent approximately 56,000 litres of Scottish organic milk south of the border to bolster supplies as the UK market tightened. Founder Bryce Cunningham said the shipment reflected unprecedented demand from English and Welsh businesses.

According to Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board figures, UK milk collections are running around 1.24 million litres lower than the same week last year. Extreme heat and drought across England and Wales have caused serious supply issues across the dairy industry.

Cunningham described the rise in demand as "quite dramatic" after receiving three calls in 10 minutes from businesses urgently seeking milk for the following week. However, when asked to supply a further 40,000 litres, the dairy could not fulfill the request.

Lost Orchards founder Angus Morrison reported a "calamity on the orchard crops for this year" down south, while Scotland has seen bumper fruit crops. He said the situation demonstrates how climate change is beginning to affect where food can be grown.

Questioning whether this constitutes a "new normal," Cunningham warned that "we can't graze animals and we can't grow food because it's too dry and too hot." He expressed concern that if such events recur frequently, future food production becomes increasingly difficult to manage.
title: England and Wales look to Scotland as drought puts pressure on milk supplies

bias: Coverage converges on hundreds of thousands of Gaza children returning to classrooms after nearly three years, often in “damaged or makeshift” buildings or tents.

The left foregrounds humanitarian deprivation, stressing “unaffordable” uniforms and supplies and near-total destruction; the right uses a more restrained, logistical frame, describing “scarce” materials while emphasizing perseverance and reopening rather than responsibility for the war.
Center coverage quantifies the devastation through UNICEF’s estimate that 98% of schools were destroyed or damaged, while de-emphasizing household shortages.
Thus, left and right share attention to material scarcity, but diverge in emotional emphasis: prolonged humanitarian hardship versus determined resumption amid constraints.
summary: On Saturday, hundreds of thousands of Palestinian children returned to in-person classes across the Gaza Strip for the first time in nearly three years, attending makeshift schools in tents and damaged buildings.

The United Nations Children's Fund reports that 98% of schools in Gaza were destroyed or damaged during the war, prompting officials to establish temporary learning centers using tents and tarpaulins.

Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan noted notebook prices surged from 3 shekels to 15 shekels due to import restrictions, while 15-year-old Samar Abu Salmi said she is "pursuing our dream" despite lacking supplies.
At least 540,000 students are expected to attend classes this year in temporary facilities, which Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis, describes as a "fragile milestone."
While in-person classes resume, online learning continues for those unable to attend, as Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using schools for military purposes, which Hamas denies.
title: Gaza students return to in-person schooling for first time in three years

bias: The center narrative foregrounds a man’s acquittal after spray-painting Churchill’s statue, using restrained legal language, while right-leaning coverage emphasizes political identity, alleged damage exceeding £7,000, and slogans such as “Free Palestine” and “Zionist war criminal.” Its rhetoric frames the act as “defaced,” “vandalised,” and “desecrated,” praises Churchill as the “greatest ever Prime Minister,” and amplifies outrage through “fumes” and “imbecile,” portraying protest as an attack on national heritage rather than expression.
The pivotal divide is whether the episode signifies lawful acquittal or cultural and patriotic affront.
Both acknowledge the jury’s not-guilty verdict, reflecting wider tensions over protest, national symbols, and Israel-Palestine politics .
summary: On Monday, a jury at Southwark Crown Court acquitted activist Caspar San Giorgi, also known as Olax Outis, of criminal damage charges after he spray-painted slogans on the Winston Churchill statue in London.

San Giorgi climbed the Parliament Square plinth on February 27, wearing a boiler suit reading "I support Palestine Action," and sprayed slogans including "Free Palestine" and "Stop the Genocide," causing an estimated £7,000 in damage.

During trial testimony, San Giorgi argued his actions constituted "preventing a crime," claiming the washable paint caused no damage and that slogans directed at Sir Keir Starmer addressed Britain's actions in Gaza.
A 10 Downing Street representative called the defacing "completely abhorrent," stating Sir Winston Churchill was a "great Briton" and the government would ensure the perpetrator was held to account.

The acquittal reflects a trend where protesters utilize "preventing a crime" defenses, complicating efforts by law enforcement and heritage bodies to secure convictions for protest-related property defacement involving public monuments.
title: Man who vandalised Churchill statue in Parliament Square found not guilty of criminal damage

summary: On Tuesday, The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group released a report warning of a "near-total absence" of effective recourse for organizations facing de-banking due to alleged ties to terrorist financing.

The report argues de-banking is a predictable outcome of Canada's anti-terror financing framework, with Muslim-led charities and NGOs operating in Syria, Palestine, or Pakistan facing disproportionate impacts.
In one instance, a humanitarian organization operating in Syria received 15 to 30 days' notice before losing services, yet "No explanation of the underlying risk was given."
Financial institutions face no legal requirement to explain account closures, and no independent body in Canada reviews whether derisking decisions are non-discriminatory or evidence-based.
The group issued a dozen recommendations for structural reform and transparency; Tim McSorley, the monitoring group's national coordinator, said "We need to see concrete policy changes.
title: Action needed to ensure groups aren't unduly 'de-banked' over terror risks: report

Center coverage neutrally notes at least 12 proposals under federal review.

summary: President Donald Trump's administration is reviewing at least 12 data center proposals covering more than 17,600 acres of public land across Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming, according to a Friday report from The Washington Sun.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum directed Bureau of Land Management officials to identify federal lands "ripe for data center development," following an executive order President Trump signed in July 2025.

Local officials and advocacy groups reported being kept in the dark about the projects, with many proposals never publicly disclosed despite polling showing 70% of Americans oppose data centers landing in their backyards.

Mary Jo Rugwell, president of the Public Lands Foundation, recently accused the administration of "bending knee to the tech oligarchs" without adequate consideration for environmental impact on public lands.

Five major technology companies received approximately $70 billion in federal tax breaks in 2025, while analysis suggests the incentives reward firms for building data centers they would construct regardless of government support.
title: Trump Considers at Least 12 Data Centers on Public Lands
